lead: Welding turns two separate pieces of metal into one continuous piece. This unit shows how each process delivers heat or pressure, what that does to the metal, and where the process is used — from a cycle frame to a car body. After this unit you can choose a process for a given job, set its main parameters, and say how the joint will be inspected.
about: The unit starts with a map. Chapter 4.1 sorts every joining process into three families: fusion, solid-state, and brazing or soldering. Chapters 4.2 and 4.3 build the two classic heat sources — the oxy-acetylene flame and the electric arc — plus the power source that feeds the arc. Chapter 4.4 spends that arc on SMAW, TIG, MIG, SAW and plasma welding, with electrodes and fluxes. Chapter 4.5 replaces the arc with Joule heating in resistance and spot welding. Chapter 4.6 joins metals without melting them at all, and 4.7 covers two modern low-heat processes, laser and cold metal transfer. Chapter 4.8 moves to brazing, soldering and adhesives, where the parent metal never melts. Chapter 4.9 closes with what goes wrong and how a joint is inspected.

chapters.idea: Every joining process is one of three things: the parent metal melts (fusion), the parent metal stays solid and is forced into contact (solid-state), or only a lower-melting filler melts (brazing and soldering).
chapters.depth: One page of classification, not process detail. Define coalescence, autogenous joint (no filler), homogeneous and heterogeneous joints, fusion zone and heat-affected zone (HAZ). Draw the three families and place each process named later in the unit under its family. Give the energy source for each family: chemical flame, electric arc, electrical resistance, high-energy beam, friction and pressure, ultrasound, explosive. Add joint types (butt, lap, T-joint, corner, edge) and weld types (groove, fillet, plug, spot, seam) only as vocabulary, and the everyday criteria for choosing a process: thickness, metal, position, production rate, distortion.
chapters.figure: Tree: root Joining, branching to Fusion (arc, gas, resistance, laser), Solid state (friction, ultrasonic, explosive, diffusion), Brazing (filler above 450 °C), Soldering (filler below 450 °C), Adhesive (no metal filler).
chapters.example: Classify these five joints and state for each whether the parent metal melts and whether a filler is used: (a) shielded metal arc welding of a mild steel butt joint, (b) friction stir welding of 6 mm aluminium plates, (c) brazing a carbide tip to a steel shank with a silver alloy melting at 700 °C, (d) resistance spot welding of two 1 mm car-body sheets, (e) soldering a PCB joint with Sn-63Pb at 183 °C. Then answer a second question: a copper-to-brass radiator joint must run at 300 °C — is solder acceptable? Answers: (a) fusion, parent melts, filler used (the electrode); (b) solid-state, parent never melts, no filler; (c) liquid-solid, only the 700 °C filler melts, parent solid; (d) fusion, a small nugget melts; (e) liquid-solid, 183 °C filler, parent solid. Solder fails at 300 °C because the joint would remelt; use a brazing alloy that melts above 300 °C and below the copper melting point.
chapters.trap: Calling brazing and soldering 'welding' — the parent never melts. And calling resistance spot welding solid-state — the nugget does melt.
chapters.leave: Solidification of the melt and the cast structure of the nugget go to Unit 1, Metal Casting Processes; the details of each process go to chapters 4.2 to 4.8.

chapters.idea: An oxy-acetylene flame gives a hot, controllable, cheap heat source, and its three flame settings are set only by the oxygen-to-acetylene ratio at the torch.
chapters.depth: Cover the gas welding station: oxygen cylinder (about 150 bar), acetylene cylinder packed with a porous mass soaked in acetone (about 15 bar), regulators, hoses with flashback arrestors, torch with a mixing chamber, interchangeable tips. Acetylene working pressure is kept low, about 1 bar or a little more, because free acetylene above roughly 1.5 bar can decompose. Flame chemistry: primary combustion in the inner cone, C₂H₂ + O₂ → 2CO + H₂, then secondary combustion in the outer envelope with more oxygen. Total requirement is 2.5 volumes of oxygen per volume of acetylene, but the neutral setting at the torch is about 1:1. Three flames and their use: neutral (about 3200 °C, steels), oxidising (brass and bronze, prevents zinc loss), carburising (high-carbon steel, hardfacing, aluminium). Leftward and rightward welding technique. Gas cutting: preheat the steel to its ignition temperature, then a pure oxygen jet burns the iron and blows the oxide out as slag; describe kerf and drag. Add oxy-hydrogen and air-acetylene as relatives.
chapters.figure: Blocks, top to bottom: oxygen cylinder and acetylene cylinder both feed regulators, then hoses, then the torch mixer, then the tip and flame.
chapters.example: An oxygen cylinder has a water capacity of 40 L and is charged to 150 bar. Treating oxygen as ideal at constant temperature, find the free oxygen at 1 bar: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, so 40 L × 150 bar = 6000 L at 1 bar = 6 m³. A neutral flame takes oxygen and acetylene in roughly 1:1 volume at the torch, so 6 m³ of acetylene is needed. An acetylene cylinder of 40 L at 15 bar holds 40 × 15 = 600 L = 0.6 m³, so one oxygen cylinder serves about 10 acetylene cylinders. If the torch consumes 300 L/h of acetylene, the oxygen cylinder lasts 6000/300 = 20 hours of welding.
chapters.trap: Saying a neutral flame is 1:1 by mass, or forgetting that 1:1 at the torch is not complete combustion — full combustion needs 2.5 volumes of oxygen per volume of acetylene. Also, the hottest point is just at the tip of the inner cone, not in the outer envelope.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for where gas welding sits among fusion processes.
chapters.leave: The physics of the arc to chapter 4.3; torch brazing and soldering to chapter 4.8.

chapters.idea: The arc is a gas made electrically conducting by ionisation, and its voltage-current curve fixes what kind of power source can hold it steady.
chapters.depth: Arc physics: thermionic emission at the cathode, ionisation of the gas column, three regions (cathode drop, plasma column, anode drop), arc temperatures of a few thousand kelvin near the metal and much higher in the column, cathode spot wandering, magnetic arc blow. Arc voltage = cathode drop + column drop + anode drop, and the column part grows with arc length. Static characteristic: voltage falls as current rises at low current, then flattens, then rises at high current. Power sources: drooping (constant current) for manual SMAW and TIG, flat (constant voltage) for MIG and SAW with the self-adjusting arc, rising for submerged arc with high current. Terms to define: open-circuit voltage (50-90 V), arc voltage (20-40 V), duty cycle, AC transformer, DC rectifier, motor-generator, inverter, DCEN and DCEP, and where the heat lands — more at the anode. Two-thirds of the heat is often quoted at the anode.
chapters.figure: Plot of voltage against current: a rising arc curve for a 5 mm arc, a steep drooping source curve, and a flat source curve; the operating point sits where the source curve crosses the arc curve.
chapters.example: A power source is rated 300 A at 60% duty cycle. Find the current it can supply continuously at 100% duty cycle. Use I²D = constant: 300² × 0.6 = I² × 1.0, so I = 300 × √0.6 = 232 A. Second part: the same machine welding at 250 A — what duty cycle is allowed? D = (300² × 0.6)/250² = 54 000/62 500 = 0.864, that is 86%, so it may weld 8.6 minutes in every 10.
chapters.trap: Taking duty cycle as a fraction of a day or of the arc time only — the standard period is 10 minutes, and the rated current is always quoted at the rated duty cycle, not at 100%.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the idea of a heat source; basic electrical circuit ideas from the physics course.
chapters.leave: Which process uses which source goes to chapter 4.4; resistance heating as a source goes to chapter 4.5; arc cutting and gouging to chapter 4.4.

chapters.idea: All arc welding processes protect the molten metal from air in a different way, and that difference decides the electrode, the gas, the thickness and the production rate.
chapters.depth: SMAW: flux-coated consumable stick, covering functions (shielding gas, slag blanket, arc stabiliser, alloying, iron powder for deposition rate), current setting, electrode designation such as E6013 and E7018 (E for electrode, first two digits the tensile strength in ksi, third the position, fourth the coating and current type), storage of low-hydrogen electrodes. TIG: non-consumable tungsten electrode (thoriated or ceriated), separate filler, argon or helium, DCEN for steel, AC for aluminium because the positive half-cycle breaks the oxide, cleaning action, thin sheet and root runs. MIG: continuous consumable wire, DCEP, CO₂ or argon-CO₂ mixtures, metal transfer modes (short circuit, globular, spray), high deposition rate, automation. SAW: arc buried under a blanket of granular flux, currents of several hundred amperes, thick plate, straight long seams. Plasma arc: arc constricted through a small nozzle, transferred and non-transferred modes, keyhole welding and cutting. Fluxes: what they do and how they are classified.
chapters.figure: Blocks, top to bottom: one root 'arc with filler' splitting into SMAW, TIG, MIG, SAW and Plasma, each with a short note on its shielding method.
chapters.example: A MIG weld runs at 200 A and 25 V with a travel speed of 5 mm/s and an arc efficiency of 0.8. Find the heat input per millimetre of weld. Heat input = efficiency × voltage × current / travel speed = 0.8 × 25 × 200 / 5 = 800 J/mm = 0.8 kJ/mm. Second part: the same joint is 6 m long — how much arc energy goes into it? 0.8 kJ/mm × 6000 mm = 4800 kJ.
chapters.trap: Thinking TIG is always filler-free (a filler rod is usually added by hand), and mixing up polarity: TIG uses DCEN for steel and AC for aluminium, while MIG uses DCEP.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.3 — the arc and its power source.
chapters.leave: Laser and cold metal transfer to chapter 4.7; arc weld defects to chapter 4.9; electron beam welding to chapter 4.7 as a relative.

chapters.idea: Resistance welding makes its own heat inside the joint by passing a large current through the contact resistance between the sheets, so the metal melts exactly where the two surfaces touch.
chapters.depth: Principle: H = I²Rt in joules, I in amperes, R in ohms, t in seconds. Where the resistance sits — electrode-to-sheet and sheet-to-sheet, with the faying surface usually the largest contact resistance at the start. Currents of 5 to 20 kA at 1 to 10 V, weld times of a few cycles to a fraction of a second, electrode force from a pneumatic or servo cylinder, copper-chromium electrodes with water cooling. The four-part cycle: squeeze, weld, hold, off. Types: spot, seam with roller electrodes and overlapping nuggets, projection, flash butt, upset, percussion. Advantages — no filler, no flux, fast, easily automated — and limits: lap joints only, shunt current through neighbouring spots, electrode wear, only thin sheets of similar metals. Nugget growth and expulsion.
chapters.figure: Gantt of one spot-weld cycle in seconds: an electrode force lane showing squeeze, weld and hold, and a current lane showing off, on, off.
chapters.example: Two 1 mm steel sheets are spot welded at 10 000 A for 0.1 s, and the total resistance between the electrodes is 100 µΩ. Find the heat generated: H = I²Rt = (10 000)² × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.1 = 1000 J. Now find the energy needed to melt a nugget of 4 mm diameter and 1.5 mm thickness: volume = π/4 × 4² × 1.5 = 18.85 mm³, mass = 18.85 × 10⁻⁹ m³ × 7850 kg/m³ = 1.48 × 10⁻⁴ kg. With specific heat 460 J/kg·K, a 1500 K rise and latent heat 270 kJ/kg: energy = 1.48 × 10⁻⁴ × (460 × 1500 + 270 000) = 142 J. So only about 14% of the generated heat forms the nugget; the rest is conducted into the electrodes and the surrounding sheet.
chapters.trap: Assuming all the generated heat melts the nugget — most of it is lost to the copper electrodes. And calling seam welding a different heat source; it is a row of overlapping spot welds.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the fusion family; chapter 4.3 for duty cycle and electrical ratings.
chapters.leave: Solid-state joining with pressure but no melting goes to chapter 4.6; nugget defects and inspection go to chapter 4.9.

chapters.idea: Solid-state joining brings two clean surfaces into intimate contact and lets pressure, heat and time make the atoms diffuse across the interface — the metal is never melted.
chapters.depth: Core idea: temperature is kept below the melting point, so there is no cast nugget and no HAZ problems of the same size. Cover: friction welding (rotary and linear, one part spins under axial force, burn-off, upset); friction stir welding (a rotating tool with a shoulder and a pin, friction and stirring raise the metal to about 0.8 of its melting point, the tool traverses, aluminium alloys, common defects such as a tunnel or a kissing bond); ultrasonic welding (20-40 kHz shear vibration under pressure, thin foils, dissimilar and plastics); explosive welding (a detonation drives one plate onto another at an angle, a jet cleans both surfaces, a wavy interface forms, used for cladding large plates); diffusion bonding (pressure, temperature and time in vacuum, titanium and ceramics — only a few universities teach this in detail); cold pressure welding and roll bonding as the deformation-based forms; joining of dissimilar metals. Say in one line that solid-state joining completes the classification of chapter 4.1.
chapters.figure: Blocks left to right: rotating tool with shoulder and pin, plunges into the plate, friction heats the metal to about 0.8 of the melting point, softened metal flows around the pin, and a stir zone is left behind with no melting.
chapters.example: Two 25 mm diameter steel rods are friction welded. The chuck turns at 1500 rpm, the axial friction pressure is 40 MPa and the coefficient of friction is 0.5. Find the rubbing speed and the friction power. Rubbing speed v = πDN/60 = π × 0.025 × 1500/60 = 1.96 m/s. Contact area A = π/4 × 0.025² = 4.91 × 10⁻⁴ m². Axial force F = 40 × 10⁶ × 4.91 × 10⁻⁴ = 19 640 N. Friction force = 0.5 × 19 640 = 9820 N. Friction power = 9820 × 1.96 = 19.3 kW.
chapters.trap: Saying friction stir welding melts the metal, and saying friction welding works only on round bars — linear friction welding joins flat parts too.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1, and the idea of plastic deformation and recrystallisation from Unit 2, Bulk Metal Forming Processes.
chapters.leave: Diffusion in solids as a materials topic goes to the materials course; ultrasonic inspection (a different use of ultrasound) goes to chapter 4.9.

chapters.idea: Laser welding gives very high power density in a very small spot, and cold metal transfer gives a controlled, very low-heat MIG arc — both exist to join thin or dissimilar parts with little distortion.
chapters.depth: Laser welding: beam sources (CO₂ at 10.6 µm, Nd:YAG at 1.06 µm, fibre laser), power density of the order of 10⁵ to 10⁷ W/cm², conduction mode against keyhole mode with a deep narrow weld, plasma plume and shielding gas, narrow HAZ, high speed, no vacuum, needs tight fit-up, poor absorption in highly reflective metals such as aluminium and copper. Add electron beam welding in two lines as the other high-energy-beam process — it needs a vacuum, which laser does not. Cold metal transfer: a modified MIG in which the wire is mechanically retracted at every short circuit, the current is cut to near zero while the drop detaches, so the arc re-ignites at low current; result is almost spatter-free transfer at low heat input, used for sheets under 1 mm, for aluminium-to-steel joints and for cladding. Only a few universities teach CMT in detail; keep it short and practical.
chapters.figure: Blocks in a cycle: arc on with the wire fed forward, short circuit with current cut, wire retracts and the drop detaches, wire advances and the arc re-ignites, with an arrow back to the start.
chapters.example: A 2 kW fibre laser welds with a spot diameter of 0.4 mm at a travel speed of 3 m/min. Find the power density and the heat input per millimetre. Spot area = π/4 × (0.4 × 10⁻³)² = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². Power density = 2000 / 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.6 × 10¹⁰ W/m² = 1.6 × 10⁶ W/cm². Travel speed = 3/60 = 0.05 m/s. Heat input = power / speed = 2000/0.05 = 40 000 J/m = 40 J/mm. Compare the 800 J/mm of the MIG example in chapter 4.4: the laser puts about 20 times less energy into each millimetre, which is why distortion is small.
chapters.trap: Thinking 'cold metal transfer' means a cold weld — it is a low-heat MIG, the metal still melts. And thinking laser welding tolerates a poor fit-up gap; it does not, because there is no filler to bridge it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3 for power density and heat input, chapter 4.4 for the MIG process that CMT modifies.
chapters.leave: Electron beam equipment detail and vacuum systems to a specialised course; laser-based additive manufacturing to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Brazing, soldering and adhesive bonding join parts with a filler that melts below the parent metal, so the parent keeps its properties and dissimilar materials can be joined.
chapters.depth: Brazing: a filler melting above 450 °C and below the parent melting point, drawn into a narrow gap by capillary action, gap of about 0.03 to 0.2 mm, lap joint design, fluxes (borax, fluorides) to dissolve oxide, heating methods (torch, furnace, induction, dip, resistance), silver-based and copper-zinc fillers, strength and service temperature. Soldering: filler melting below 450 °C, tin-lead eutectic at 183 °C, lead-free alloys around 217-230 °C, rosin fluxes, hand soldering and wave or reflow soldering in electronics, why the joint is weak and cannot take high temperature. Adhesive bonding: the joint is a polymer layer, mechanisms quoted as mechanical interlocking, adsorption and diffusion, surface preparation, lap shear loading, advantages with thin sheets, dissimilar metals and composites, limits of temperature, creep and ageing. End with a comparison table: heat, parent melting, filler, joint strength, typical use.
chapters.figure: Stack of joining methods from hottest at the top to coolest at the bottom: welding where the parent melts, brazing where the filler melts above 450 °C, soldering with filler below 450 °C, adhesive with no metal filler.
chapters.example: A brazed lap joint has a gap of d = 0.05 mm between parallel plates. The filler has surface tension γ = 0.4 N/m, contact angle θ = 30°, and density 8000 kg/m³. Estimate the capillary rise with h = 2γcosθ/(ρgd). Numerator = 2 × 0.4 × 0.866 = 0.693 N/m. Denominator = 8000 × 9.81 × 5 × 10⁻⁵ = 3.92 N/m². So h = 0.177 m, about 177 mm. Explain why real joints fill only a few millimetres: air trapped in the gap, oxide on the metal, and the filler freezing as it meets cold metal. The lesson is to keep the clearance small but not zero, and to use a flux.
chapters.trap: Saying brazing or soldering melts the parent metal, and forgetting the 450 °C line that separates the two. Also thinking a soldered joint can carry the same load or temperature as a brazed one.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the third family of joining; chapter 2 for torch heating.
chapters.leave: The metallurgy of filler alloys goes to a materials course; electronics assembly processes go to an electronics course.

chapters.idea: Most weld defects come from the three things a weld must control — heat, cleanliness and protection from air — and each defect has a standard inspection method that can see it.
chapters.depth: Defects with cause and remedy: porosity (damp electrode, dirty surface, gas entrapment), slag inclusion (poor inter-run cleaning, wrong technique), incomplete fusion and incomplete penetration (low current, fast travel, wrong joint gap), undercut (excess current, long arc, wrong angle), overlap, spatter, burn-through, arc strike, distortion and residual stress, and cracks — hot cracks that form while solidifying, cold or hydrogen-induced cracks that appear hours later, crater cracks, lamellar tearing in thick plate. Remedies: correct current and polarity, dry electrodes, preheat, post-weld heat treatment, proper bead sequence. Inspection: visual, dye penetrant for surface flaws, magnetic particle for surface and near-surface flaws in steel, ultrasonic for planar flaws deep inside, radiography for volumetric flaws such as porosity and slag, plus destructive tests — bend test, nick-break, tensile, hardness and macro-section. Acceptance criteria: what a code limits, in general terms.
chapters.figure: Tree: root 'weld defects' branching to cracks (hot, cold, crater), porosity, slag inclusion, incomplete fusion, undercut, and distortion.
chapters.example: An ultrasonic test on a 20 mm thick butt weld shows a single echo at t = 4.07 µs after the pulse, with the shear wave speed in steel c = 5900 m/s. Find the depth of the reflector. The wave travels down and back, so d = c × t / 2 = 5900 × 4.07 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 0.0120 m = 12.0 mm. The flaw lies 12 mm below the surface, in the root region of the weld, and would be reported as a lack of penetration unless a second probe angle shows it to be something else.
chapters.trap: Mixing up incomplete fusion with incomplete penetration, and expecting radiography to find every crack — radiography is good for porosity and slag but can miss a tight crack lying parallel to the beam.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 — the processes that produce these defects.
chapters.leave: Casting defects, which follow the same logic, go to Unit 1; measurement of residual stress goes to a testing course.
